html:
The empire of the Safavid dynasty, which ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736 and made Twelver Shia Islam its state religion. That choice still shapes Iran and the map of Islam today.

The Safavids began as the hereditary sheikhs of a Sufi order at Ardabil, in northwest Iran. Their Turkmen followers, the Qizilbash or "red heads", were fiercely devoted to them. In 1501 the fourteen-year-old Ismail took Tabriz and crowned himself shah. He imposed Shiism on a mostly Sunni population and brought in Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach it.

The new faith put Iran at odds with the Sunni Ottoman Empire. The Ottomans beat Ismail at Chaldiran in 1514, and the two empires fought on and off for more than a century. Their border roughly became today's border between Iran and Turkey and Iraq.

The greatest shah was Abbas I (1588 to 1629). He built an army of slave soldiers loyal only to him, took back land from the Ottomans, and with English ships drove the Portuguese from Hormuz in 1622. He moved the capital to Isfahan and built its great square, with the Shah Mosque on one side. Armenian merchants he settled there ran the silk trade to Europe.

Safavid court art was rich in painting and carpets; the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp is one of the finest illustrated books ever made. Tahmasp also sheltered the exiled Mughal emperor Humayun, who took Persian painters back to India.

The dynasty weakened in the late 1600s. Afghan rebels took Isfahan in 1722, and the general Nadir Shah ended Safavid rule in 1736.
sum: The empire of the Safavid dynasty, which ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736 and made Twelver Shia Islam its state religion. That choice still shapes Iran and the map of Islam today.
